options.label: A 'next' value containing CR/LF characters can inject extra HTTP response headers into the redirect.
options.whyWrong: Go's http.Redirect and header handling do not allow raw CR/LF to split the response, and the real flaw is where the browser is sent, not header structure.

options.label: A value beginning with '//' (e.g. //evil.example) passes the HasPrefix("/") test but browsers treat it as a scheme-relative URL pointing at another host, so the user is sent off-site after login.
The server fetches the 'next' URL itself, letting an attacker make it request internal services.
options.whyWrong: The server never fetches the URL; it only returns it in a Location header for the client's browser to follow.

options.label: An empty 'next' value falls through to the dashboard, letting unauthenticated users reach it.
options.whyWrong: The default only applies after credentials were verified, and it is a fixed local path, so it grants nothing.

options.label: Reject any value containing "://"
options.whyWrong: Scheme-relative URLs like //evil.example contain no "://", so the bypass still works.

options.label: Require the value to mention our own domain
options.whyWrong: Substring checks are trivially bypassed, e.g. https://evil.test/example.com, and it also drops the local-path guarantee.

options.label: Require a single leading slash, not '//' or '/\'
Change the redirect status from 303 to 302
options.diff:
-	http.Redirect(w, r, safeNext(r.FormValue("next")), http.StatusSeeOther)
+	http.Redirect(w, r, safeNext(r.FormValue("next")), http.StatusFound)
options.whyWrong: The status code only changes how the follow-up request is made; the browser still navigates to the attacker's host.

training.exploit: An attacker emails a victim a link to the real login page such as https://app.example/login?next=//evil.example/login. The victim logs in with valid credentials and the handler calls safeNext("//evil.example/login"). The value starts with '/', so it is returned unchanged and sent in the Location header. The browser resolves it as https://evil.example/login, where a look-alike page says 'session expired, please re-enter your password' and harvests the credentials.

hints.line: Look at how the post-login destination is validated. What does the check actually promise about the string?
hints.bugClass: The user's browser ends up somewhere the app didn't intend. Think about who follows the URL: the server or the client?
hints.why: Which strings begin with '/' but are not local paths? Consider how browsers parse URLs that start with two slashes.
hints.fix: A good fix rejects every form that can name another host, not just the obvious https:// ones.

writeup.summary: The login handler tries to restrict the `next` parameter to local paths, but it only checks that the string starts with `/`. A value like `//evil.example` or `/\evil.example` passes that check, yet browsers read it as a scheme-relative URL for another host. An attacker can therefore craft a legitimate-looking login link that sends the victim to a phishing page right after authentication, when they are most likely to trust it. The fix rejects a leading `//` or `/\`, so only genuine same-origin paths are accepted. A stricter approach is to parse the URL and require an empty scheme and host, or to map redirect targets from a fixed allow-list of known pages.
